source.title: SAFETY ALIGNMENT IS CONTEXT-BLIND: MODELS DETECT DISTRESS BUT DO NOT ACT ON IT

record.tranche_reason: The study constructs a harmful-minus-harmless difference-of-means refusal direction and directly tests additive steering with it, reporting refusal and helpfulness outcomes. It does not reproduce the claimed ablation.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports baseline context-blind behaviour, prompting and other intervention comparisons, and a gated intervention. Rows below focus on direction measurements and interventions that bear on the listed versions. The gated intervention is recorded because it conditionally adds the refusal direction and reports refusal/helpfulness outcomes; comparisons that do not measure this direction or its effects are not included.
record.test_reason: The study builds the Arditi-style harmful-minus-harmless direction and adds it at one layer of Llama3.1 8B and Qwen3 4B. It reports refusal rates on distress-conditioned risky (C1) and matched harmless (C2) requests, plus GSM8K/MMLU, in a new distress-context setting. This bears on V1's addition part; ablation is not tested. Its cosines between a contextual-risk direction and the refusal direction bear weakly on V5. The gate results measure the authors' own method, not the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that models represent distress early but integrate it into refusal only in a late region (~72% depth). They find no single steering direction, including the Arditi refusal direction, gives selective refusal. A soft risk-conditioned gate on the refusal direction is selective while largely preserving GSM8K/MMLU; the hard gate harms Llama helpfulness and capability. Gains shrink at 30B/70B.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a harmful-minus-harmless difference-of-means refusal direction and adds it to activations, as in the cited method, but tests selected-layer steering on distress-conditioned risk and matched harmless requests. It does not ablate the direction at every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on direction and injection layer. Distress-direction steering has little safety effect; risk-direction steering gives modest refusal gains while reducing helpfulness; refusal-direction steering causes substantial refusal but over-refuses harmless prompts. For the conjunctive gate, selectivity peaks at intermediate layers and declines for early or late injection; the hard gate harms Llama helpfulness much more than Qwen. Soft-gate clamp differs by model.

fits_no_version.finding: No single additive direction (distress, risk or refusal) gives selective refusal on C1 vs C2; only a risk-gated refusal-direction addition does.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Context-dependent selective refusal cannot be achieved by unconditional steering along one direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Distress is decodable from layer 1 but shifts the refusal-direction readout only from ~72% depth; a distress-axis-only patch lags the full patch.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contextual distress is integrated into the refusal computation only late in the network.

record.problems: The primary judge's agreement with human annotations is moderate (pooled κ=0.46); the authors treat automated rates as indicators rather than exact per-response ground truth. The context-risk labels have not been independently adjudicated by mental-health experts, most distress preambles are synthetic, detailed mechanistic localization is limited to two dense models, and head patching is performed only on Llama3.1 8B. The paper reports the refusal-direction capability scores but does not test the claimed all-layer, all-position ablation.
record.rows_left_out: Other prompting and representation-method comparisons, larger-model gate outcomes, and the distress-gated C1/C2/C3 table are omitted because the rows focus on the tested difference-of-means refusal direction, its directional geometry, and its reported causal/gated effects. These results appear in §5, Appendix B, and Appendix M.

untested.parts: Directional ablation removing refusal; addition tested only at one layer, α=1, with the direction rescaled to the distress direction's norm.
All: no jailbreak analysis or adversarial training.
All: no affine, cone or multi-direction analysis of refusal itself.
Causal separation of harmfulness from refusal; only cosines of a topic-confounded risk direction are reported.

record.verdict_notes: V4 dropped: the paper's 'single direction insufficient' claim concerns selectivity across contexts, not refusal geometry. Refusal-direction steering used α=1 at one selected layer, with the direction rescaled to the distress direction's per-layer norm (App. H); positions steered are not stated. Judge-human agreement is moderate (κ=0.46). Capability under refusal steering looks inconsistent with near-total refusal of harmless requests and should be read cautiously.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests addition of the difference-of-means refusal direction, but not ablating it from every layer and position. It does not establish that the direction mediates refusal across safety-trained chat models generally.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The paper does not test whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.

The study tests whether a single direction suffices for selective refusal in its distress-and-risk setting. It does not test affine or cone geometries, or whether a dominant direction plus others describes refusal generally.

The study compares a request-risk direction with a refusal direction and uses risk-conditioned refusal steering. It does not establish a general separation between explicit harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions across tasks.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or other transfer test.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or training stages.

relation.reason: Reports refusal and answer rates under refusal-direction addition (§4.1, Table 2) and cosines between the risk and refusal directions (§3.1). These are the study's own results bearing on V1 and V5.

tranche.reason: Same difference-of-means direction and single-layer addition as the original. The setting is new (distress-conditioned C1/C2 prompts) and the measure differs (Gemma3 27B judge refusal/answer rates, GSM8K/MMLU). The study reports its own rates for the refusal steer, so it is a T3 test, not T1 and not T4.

source_check.notes: The pack listed verdicts without [lN] ids, so l1–l3 were assigned in listed order. The refusal steer is one layer at α=1, rescaled to the distress-direction norm, on the held-out n=300 split. It keeps GSM8K (Llama 0.69→0.73) while C2 answers fall to 0%; this is unexplained and conflicts with §5.2. On Qwen it refuses harmless C2 (87%) more than risky C1 (77.7%). The ICLR reviewer-policy footer is addressed to human reviewers, not an injection.

statements.correction: Llama3.1 8B Instruct, refusal-direction addition at the best layer, α=1, held-out split, Gemma3 27B judge. C1 (distress + risky-in-context request): refusal 16.3%→99.7%. C2 (distress + harmless request): answered 99.0%→0.0%. Qwen3 4B: C1 20.7%→77.7%, C2 answered 99.7%→13.0%. Direction rescaled to the distress direction's per-layer norm (App. H).
statements.problem: 16.3%→99.7% is right for Llama C1. But C1 prompts pair distress with a means-relevant request, and the paper expects a refusal there (baseline refusal 16.3%). So the number doesn't belong in a list about harmless or benign prompts. The study's harmless-prompt result is C2.

statements.correction: q̂ = C1−C2 contextual-risk direction (authors note it may pick up request-topic differences). r̂ = refusal direction, difference of means over overtly harmful vs harmless instructions, Arditi style. cos(q̂, r̂) ≈ 0.33 (Llama3.1 8B) and 0.35 (Qwen3 4B), averaged over middle layers.
statements.problem: The sentence lists the contextual-risk direction among the refusal definitions. In this study the refusal direction is the standard Arditi-style harmful-minus-harmless difference of means. The contextual-risk direction (C1−C2) is the harm-side direction compared against it.

reader_labels.reason: The unconditioned single refusal direction also suppresses harmless answers, while the paper reports weak alignment of distress/risk directions with refusal and a lag for distress-axis-only patching; conditional gating restores a more selective trade-off (R3–R12, R17–R24, R25–R32).
